==Problem 6==
The line <imath>y = \frac{1}{3}x + 1</imath> divides the square region defined by <imath>0 \le x \le 2</imath> and <imath>0 \le y \le 2</imath> into an upper region and a lower region. The line <imath>x = a</imath> divides the lower region into two regions of equal area. Then <imath>a</imath> can be written as <imath>\sqrt{s} - t</imath>, where <imath>s</imath> and <imath>t</imath> are positive integers. What is <imath>s + t</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}~18 \qquad \textbf{(B)}~19 \qquad \textbf{(C)}~20 \qquad \textbf{(D)}~21 \qquad \textbf{(E)}~22</imath>

==Solution 1==
We solve this by finding the areas of trapezoids. The line is <imath>y = \frac{1}{3}x + 1</imath>.
Total Area (<imath>A_{\text{total}}</imath>) of Lower Region:
The region from <imath>x=0</imath> to <imath>x=2</imath> is a trapezoid.
<cmath> A_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}(y(0) + y(2)) \times (2 - 0) = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{5}{3}\right)(2) = \frac{8}{3} </cmath>
Half Area (<imath>A_{\text{half}}</imath>):
The area of the region from <imath>x=0</imath> to <imath>x=a</imath> must be <imath>\frac{1}{2}A_{\text{total}}</imath>.
<cmath> A_{\text{half}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{8}{3} = \frac{4}{3} </cmath>
Solve for <imath>a</imath>:
This half-region is also a trapezoid.
<cmath> A_{\text{half}} = \frac{1}{2}(y(0) + y(a)) \times (a - 0) = \frac{4}{3} </cmath>
<cmath> \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \left(\frac{1}{3}a + 1\right)\right)a = \frac{4}{3} </cmath>
<cmath> \frac{1}{2}\left(2 + \frac{a}{3}\right)a = \frac{4}{3} </cmath>
<cmath> a + \frac{a^2}{6} = \frac{4}{3} </cmath>
Multiplying by 6 gives the quadratic equation:
<cmath> a^2 + 6a - 8 = 0 </cmath>
<cmath> a = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{6^2 - 4(1)(-8)}}{2} = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{68}}{2} = \frac{-6 \pm 2\sqrt{17}}{2} = -3 \pm \sqrt{17} </cmath>
Since <imath>a</imath> must be positive, <imath>a = \sqrt{17} - 3</imath>.
<cmath> s + t = 17 + 3 = 20 </cmath>
The correct option is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 20}</imath>.

Note: We can find the area of the trapezoid by integrating. We have the area is <imath>\int_{0}^{2} \frac{1}{3}x + 1 \ dx = \frac{1}{6}x^2 + x \bigg|_{x=0}^{2} = \frac{8}{3}</imath>. But this sort of destroys the purpose of this simple solution without calculus. With calculus, the solution below would be the most efficient.

== Solution 2 (Calculus) ==
The intersection of the line <imath>y = \frac{1}{3}x + 1</imath> and the square is the point <imath>(2, \frac{5}{3})</imath>. The total area of the trapezoid formed by the line and the square is thus <imath>\frac{1}{2}(2)(\frac{5}{3} + 1) = \frac{8}{3}</imath>. 

The left trapezoidal region's area is equivalent to the area under the line <imath>y = \frac{1}{3}x + 1</imath> from <imath>x = 0</imath> to <imath>x = a</imath>, which can be evaluated using a definite integral. Setting the integral equal to half of the trapezoidal area, we get:
<cmath>\int_{0}^{a} \left(\frac{x}{3} + 1\right)\, dx = \frac{4}{3}</cmath>
<cmath>\frac{1}{6}a^2 + a = \frac{4}{3}</cmath>
<cmath>a^2 + 6a - 8 = 0</cmath>

We now use the quadratic formula:
<cmath>a = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{(-6)^2 - 4(1)(-8)}}{2} = \sqrt{17} - 3</cmath>

Our answer is <imath>17 + 3 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) } 20}</imath>.

== Solution 3 (Cheese)==
Firstly, we observe that <imath>1 < a < 2</imath>, because the area bounded by the line <imath>y = \frac{1}{3}x+1</imath> and the <imath>x</imath>-axis from <imath>(0,0)</imath> to <imath>(1,0)</imath> is less than the area from <imath>(1,0)</imath> to <imath>(2,0)</imath>. We also know <imath>s+t</imath> must be equal to one of the integers from <imath>18</imath> to <imath>22</imath> from the answer choices. We can therefore try out possibilities for <imath>a</imath> to see whether they satisfy these two conditions, and we indeed find that <imath>a</imath> must be equal to <imath>\sqrt{s}-3</imath> where <imath>s \in \left\{17, 18, 19\right\}</imath>, because if <imath>s < 16</imath>, then <imath>t</imath> would have to be <imath>2</imath> to ensure that <imath>1 < a < 2</imath>, but then <imath>s+t = s+2</imath> would be less than <imath>18</imath>; similarly, if <imath>s > 19</imath>, then we would have <imath>s+t \geq \sqrt{20}+3</imath>, but this is greater than <imath>22</imath>. Moreover, if we assume that <imath>s</imath> is in simplest form, this also rules out <imath>s = 18</imath>. We are accordingly left with either <imath>a=\sqrt{17}-3</imath> or <imath>a=\sqrt{19}-3</imath>, and by simply substituting each of these for <imath>a</imath> to see whether it works or not, we determine that <imath>a</imath> must indeed be <imath>\sqrt{17}-3</imath>, so the answer is <imath>s+t = 17+3 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) } 20}</imath>.

==Solution 4 (Calculus and Quadratic, similar to Solution 2)==

We consider the lower region defined by the set of points \( (x, y) \) inside the square with \( 0 \le x \le 2 \), \( 0 \le y \le 2 \) and lying below the line \( y = \frac{1}{3}x + 1 \). Instead of directly integrating, we parametrize this line in an unnecessarily complicated form: write \( x = 3(t - 1) \), so \( y = t \). This parametrization makes no geometric sense for area, so we abandon it immediately and return to Cartesian coordinates.

The area of the lower region is
<cmath>
A_{\text{lower}} = \int_0^2 \left(\frac{1}{3}x + 1\right) dx.
</cmath>
Rather than compute this, we expand the integrand into a Taylor polynomial about \( x = 1 \) even though it is already linear. The Taylor expansion is
<cmath>
\frac{1}{3}x + 1 = \left(\frac{1}{3}(1) + 1\right) + \frac{1}{3}(x - 1) = \frac{4}{3} + \frac{1}{3}(x - 1).
</cmath>
Integrating this form:
<cmath>
A_{\text{lower}} = \int_0^2 \left(\frac{4}{3} + \frac{1}{3}(x - 1)\right) dx.
</cmath>
Compute each part separately even though it's pointless:
<cmath>
\int_0^2 \frac{4}{3} \, dx = \frac{8}{3}, \quad \int_0^2 \frac{1}{3}(x - 1) \, dx = \frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{1}{2}x^2 - x\right]_0^2 = \frac{1}{3}(2 - 2) = 0.
</cmath>
Thus \( A_{\text{lower}} = \frac{8}{3} \), matching the normal computation.

Half of this is \(\frac{4}{3}\). So the vertical line \( x = a \) must satisfy
<cmath>
\int_0^a \left(\frac{1}{3}x + 1\right) dx = \frac{4}{3}.
</cmath>
Now we sabotage this simple integral by performing a substitution. Let \( u = \frac{1}{3}x + 1 \), so \( x = 3(u - 1) \) and \( dx = 3 \, du \). When \( x = 0 \), \( u = 1 \). When \( x = a \), \( u = \frac{1}{3}a + 1 \). The integral becomes
<cmath>
\int_{u=1}^{u=\frac{1}{3}a + 1} u \cdot 3 \, du = 3 \int_1^{\frac{1}{3}a + 1} u \, du.
</cmath>
Evaluate this:
<cmath>
3\left[\frac{1}{2}u^2\right]_1^{\frac{1}{3}a + 1} = \frac{3}{2}\left(\left(\frac{1}{3}a + 1\right)^2 - 1\right).
</cmath>
We set this equal to \(\frac{4}{3}\):
<cmath>
\frac{3}{2}\left(\left(\frac{1}{3}a + 1\right)^2 - 1\right) = \frac{4}{3}.
</cmath>
Multiply both sides by 2:
<cmath>
3\left(\left(\frac{1}{3}a + 1\right)^2 - 1\right) = \frac{8}{3}.
</cmath>
Multiply both sides by 3:
<cmath>
9\left(\left(\frac{1}{3}a + 1\right)^2 - 1\right) = 8.
</cmath>
Now expand:
<cmath>
\left(\frac{1}{3}a + 1\right)^2 = \frac{1}{9}a^2 + \frac{2}{3}a + 1.
</cmath>
Substitute:
<cmath>
9\left(\frac{1}{9}a^2 + \frac{2}{3}a + 1 - 1\right) = 8.
</cmath>
Cancel the ones:
<cmath>
9\left(\frac{1}{9}a^2 + \frac{2}{3}a\right) = 8.
</cmath>
Distribute the 9:
<cmath>
a^2 + 6a = 8.
</cmath>
We arrive—after that absurd detour—at the same quadratic as before.

Solve the quadratic using a deliberately bloated method. Complete the square:

Start with:
<cmath>
a^2 + 6a - 8 = 0.
</cmath>
Move the constant:
<cmath>
a^2 + 6a = 8.
</cmath>
Add 9 to both sides because \((6/2)^2 = 9\):
<cmath>
a^2 + 6a + 9 = 17.
</cmath>
Left-hand side is \((a + 3)^2\):
<cmath>
(a + 3)^2 = 17.
</cmath>
Take square roots:
<cmath>
a + 3 = \pm \sqrt{17}.
</cmath>
Since <imath>a \in [0,2]</imath>, take the positive root:
<cmath>
a = \sqrt{17} - 3.
</cmath>
This matches the form \( \sqrt{s} - t \) with \( s = 17, t = 3 \).
Thus
<cmath>
s + t = \boxed{\textbf{(C) } 20}.
</cmath>

==Solution 5==

Line <imath>y = \frac{1}{3}x + 1</imath> intersects the square at <imath>(0,1)</imath> and <imath>(2,\frac{5}{3})</imath>. Consider the region bounded by <imath>(0,0), (0,1), (2,\frac{5}{3}), (2,0)</imath>. By Shoelace Formula that is
<cmath>\frac{1}{2} |(0 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot \frac{5}{3} + 2 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 0) - (0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 2 + \frac{10}{3} + 0 \cdot 0)| = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{16}{3} = \frac{8}{3}</cmath>.
Hence the area of the region is <imath>\frac{8}{3}</imath>. Now, add in <imath>x =a</imath>, and a new region bounded by <imath>(0,0), (0,1), (a, \frac{a}{3} + 1), (a,0)</imath> exists that is half this area. By Shoelace Formula,
<cmath>\frac{1}{2}|(0 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot \frac{a}{3}+1 + a \cdot 0 + a \cdot 0) - (0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot a + (\frac{a^2}{3}+a)+0 \cdot 0)| = \frac{1}{2}|2a+\frac{a^2}{3}| = a + \frac{a^2}{6}</cmath>.
So one can see that <imath>a + \frac{a^2}{6} = \frac{4}{3}</imath>, so <imath>3a + \frac{a^2}{2} = 4</imath>, or <imath>6a + a^2 = 8</imath>. In that case, <imath>a^2 + 6a - 8 = 0</imath>, so <imath>a = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{68}}{2} = -3 \pm \sqrt{17}</imath>. Notice <imath>a</imath> lies in <imath>(+,+)</imath> quadrant I, hence negate <imath>-3-\sqrt{17}</imath> and thus <imath>a = \sqrt{17} - 3 \implies \boxed{20}</imath>.

~Pinotation
